The bottle arrived on a Tuesday, which was the kind of day the sea preferred for its small cruelties.

Eamon Voss had kept the Harrow Point light for eleven years. Eleven years of climbing the one hundred and twelve iron steps each evening, eleven years of trimming the wick, eleven years of watching the fog roll in from the north like a slow grey animal. He knew the rhythm of the rocks below his tower, the way the tide pulled back and whispered secrets into the crevices, the way the gulls argued over scraps of bread he'd never thrown.

So when he found the bottle wedged between two boulders at the waterline—green glass, cork-stoppered, salt-crusted like a relic from some drowned century—he felt the old pull. The one that said *this is not nothing.*

He carried it up the steps. Set it on the brass railing of the lantern room, where the great lens turned its slow golden eye over the dark water. He pried the cork with his thumbnail. Inside, a strip of paper, folded three times, the ink faded to the color of weak tea.

# The Keeper of Harrow Point

The fog had not lifted in three days.

Elias Vane stood at the base of the spiral staircase, his boots slick with salt, and watched the beam of the lighthouse carve its slow arc through the grey. Forty-one years he'd kept the light at Harrow Point. Forty-one years of the same rhythm: wind, wave, wick, and the endless grey sea pressing against the rocks like a patient animal.

He was mending a torn section of the gallery railing when he saw it.

It sat wedged between two boulders at the waterline, half-buried in kelp and the pale foam of a receding tide. A bottle. Green glass, thick as a child's thumb, its cork swollen and black with brine. Elias knelt, his knees protesting, and pried it free.

Inside, a rolled slip of paper.

He dried it on his coat for an hour before he could read the ink. The handwriting was small, cramped, the letters pressed hard into the page as though the writer had been in a hurry or in fear.

*To whoever finds this — I am Maren. I am on the island. I have been here eleven days. The boat did not come. The boat will not come. If you can read this, please tell them I am still breathing. Please tell them my name. — M.*

Elias read it four times.

He walked back up the one hundred and twelve steps to the lantern room, set the paper on the brass table beside his logbook, and stared at the sea. The fog swallowed everything beyond the breakwater. There was no island to be seen. There was no island *to be seen*, he reminded himself, but the charts in the keeper's cottage spoke of a small rock called Maren's Tooth, three miles south-southwest, where the current ran strange and the old fishing boats sometimes lost their bearings.

He had not seen a soul on that rock in twenty years.

# The Keeper of Harrow Point

The bottle washed up on a Tuesday, which was the kind of day that made Elias Vane feel the weight of the lighthouse pressing down on his shoulders. Gray sky. Gray sea. The same gray he'd worn for eleven years, from the salt-stiffened wool of his coat to the film of it in his eyes.

He was mending the net along the eastern rocks when he saw it—green glass, half-buried in the kelp, catching what little light the clouds allowed. He pulled it free. The cork was swollen with brine but held. Inside, a rolled slip of paper, dark with age.

Elias sat on the cold stone, his hands trembling in a way he hadn't felt since Margaret left. He pried the cork free with his thumbnail and unrolled the paper.

*To whoever finds this: I am Thomas Wren, keeper of Harrow Point Light, 1923. The storms are worse this year. I have not spoken to another soul in four months. If you are reading this, know that the light still burns. Know that I am still here. Know that the sea does not take everything, even if it feels like it does.*
